KTPH000Input hardeningKTPH001 asks the AI to build an KTPH002input-validation guard blockKTPH003 directly into a script it generates or rewrites. The guard runs at the very top of the script, before any real work, and rejects bad input on the host that executes the script: wrong parameter counts, forbidden characters, oversized values, missing input files, files in the wrong format, and files above a configurable size limit. Violations stop the script with a clear message and a documented exit code — unless the run is deliberately forced.
The guard lives in the script, not in korTTY

korTTY performs KTPH000no validation of its ownKTPH001 when a snippet or workflow script runs. Input hardening changes the KTPH002scriptKTPH003: the AI writes the checks into the code, so they protect every future run of that script — also when it is started outside korTTY, by a scheduler, or on a remote host. If you edit the script later, the guard is ordinary script code you can read, adjust, or remove.

Despite the similar name, this is a different feature than KTPH001Hardening optionsKTPH002. KTPH003Hardening optionsKTPH004 are general production-quality techniques (strict mode, error traps, logging, KTPH000, …) that shape KTPH005how the script is writtenKTPH006. KTPH007Input hardeningKTPH008 is about KTPH009what the script acceptsKTPH010: it adds a concrete guard block that validates parameters and input files at run time. The two panels appear side by side and can be combined freely.
The KTPH000Input hardeningKTPH001 panel shows up in the same places as the classic hardening panel, plus the AI-Swarm generator:
KTPH000Terminal → Generate Workflow ScriptKTPH001 (the KTPH002WorkflowKTPH003 button after an agent run)
KTPH000Snippet editor → AI Code → Improve robustnessKTPH001
KTPH000Snippet editor → AI Code → Custom improvement…KTPH001
KTPH000Snippet editor → AI Code → Full code analysisKTPH001
You click KTPH000Apply selectedKTPH001; each enabled guard rule becomes a separately tracked mandatory requirement, and an incomplete replacement is rejected before review

Unlike the classic hardening options, input hardening is KTPH000strictly opt-inKTPH001: the master check box starts unticked and the panel starts collapsed, because the guard changes the script's runtime behaviour — a script that previously accepted any input will start rejecting input that violates the rules. Tick KTPH002Input hardening (validate script inputs)KTPH003 to activate it for the current generation or rewrite.

Declarative YAML/YML/Ansible targets cannot receive this imperative argument-and-file guard. KorTTY disables the panel for those targets in the workflow, swarm, KTPH000Improve robustnessKTPH001, KTPH002Custom improvementKTPH003, and KTPH004Full code analysisKTPH005 dialogs, and an already-saved enabled default yields no effective guard configuration there. For snippet improvements in a supported language, enabling Input hardening changes the target to the KTPH006complete snippetKTPH007 so the guard can be placed before all real work; the complete result is reviewed before it is applied.
With the master check box ticked, five sub-options control what the guard enforces. All five are pre-ticked; untick what you do not want.

Every parameter the script is called with is validated: the exact expected parameter count, a per-parameter character allowlist derived from how the script actually uses the value (a number, a file path, a host name, a keyword, free text), and a maximum length per parameter. Control characters, NUL bytes and shell metacharacters (KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003, KTPH004, KTPH005, KTPH006, KTPH007, embedded newlines) are rejected for every parameter that does not legitimately need them, so over-long or maliciously crafted values are refused instead of processed.

Every parameter the script uses as an input file path is checked before first use: the file must exist and be readable, and its content format must match what the script can process. A text-processing script rejects binary files — the guard scans the first bytes for NUL bytes and additionally consults KTPH000 only where that command exists, falling back to the built-in check where it does not.

The guard defines a KTPH000 variable (in bytes) in its configuration section. When KTPH001 is greater than KTPH002, the guard obtains the file size from metadata before any operation reads file content — including the format check's initial content scan. A larger file is rejected with exit code KTPH003 and its content is not read. If no metadata-only size query is available, the guard rejects the file without reading it. KTPH004 means unlimited and skips the size check entirely. The size spinner in the panel accepts KTPH005–KTPH006 MB and sets the generated default to 10 MB unless you change it.
Security warnings to stderr KTPH001 script logKTPH000

Every violation is reported as a timestamped security warning line starting with KTPH000 on stderr. If KTPH001FORCE=1 / --force overrideKTPH002 is also selected, every forced bypass is reported the same way. If the script writes its own log file, the guard appends the same warning line there too, so the script's log carries a complete security trail.

Blocking is the default, but a run can be forced: when the environment variable KTPH000 is set to KTPH001 or the script is invoked with the KTPH002 parameter, the guard downgrades every violation to a warning and continues. The guard accepts KTPH003 anywhere on the command line and excludes it from parameter validation. Each individual violation is still reported, plus one extra warning that enforcement was bypassed — a forced run always leaves a complete trace.

When the guard blocks a run (and no force override is active), it uses distinct, documented exit codes so callers can tell KTPH002whyKTPH003 the input was rejected. The prompt names only codes created by the selected checks: format-only and size-only selections each describe only their own KTPH000 case, and KTPH001 is included only with KTPH004Input file format checksKTPH005.
A parameter violated the rules (count, characters, length)
An input file failed the format or size checks
An input file is missing or unreadable

The guard uses each language's own built-ins and standard library wherever available, and it probes optional platform tools before using them. Bash guards use KTPH000, pattern matching, GNU KTPH001 or BSD/macOS KTPH002 for a metadata-only size check, and a NUL-byte scan only after that size check passes; if neither KTPH003 form works, the guard rejects the file without reading it. Python guards use KTPH004, KTPH005, KTPH006 and a binary read; Perl guards use KTPH007, untainting regex allowlists, taint mode (KTPH008) where the script allows it and the metadata-only KTPH009 operator; Ruby guards use KTPH010, KTPH011, KTPH012 and KTPH013. Other script languages get generic guidance only for the native argument, file, logging or environment facilities required by the selected sub-options. Declarative YAML/YML/Ansible targets are disabled because they take no positional parameters this way.

Below the sub-options, KTPH001AllKTPH002 and KTPH003ClearKTPH004 tick or untick every sub-option, and KTPH005SaveKTPH006 remembers the master toggle, the sub-option set and the size limit as your default — every Input hardening panel then opens with that selection. The panel title in the Full code analysis window shows a live KTPH007countKTPH008 of the effectively active sub-options, which is KTPH000 while the master toggle is off.
